title: Electrolytes Before or After Drinking? Timing That Actually Helps
excerpt: Should you take electrolytes before, during, or after drinking? What your kidneys do with alcohol on board, why bedtime and morning matter most, and what rehydration can't fix.
metaDescription: Should you drink electrolytes before or after drinking? What your kidneys do with alcohol, and and when electrolytes help most: before, during, or after.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The answer first:** after drinking matters more than before. The most useful times for an electrolyte drink are right before bed and the next morning, because that is when you are actually short on fluid. Before you drink, a normal salty meal and some water do the same job as any pre-loading routine, since your kidneys simply flush out extra salt you don't need yet. During the night, the main benefit of an electrolyte drink or a glass of water between rounds is that it slows you down. And at every stage, keep your expectations honest: rehydrating helps with thirst, dry mouth, and some of the headache, but it does not prevent or cure a hangover.

This guide is about *when*. If you're trying to decide *which* drink to buy, our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) goes through the labels side by side, and our [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) guide ranks the wider field. Here we focus on what your body, and especially your kidneys, are doing with alcohol on board at each point in the night, and what that means for timing.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research in plain language. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor before using electrolyte drinks regularly if** you have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure and have been told to limit sodium or potassium, or you take medicines that affect potassium. **Get medical help if** you can't keep fluids down for more than a day, you feel faint when you stand, you are confused, or you are passing very little urine. If someone can't be woken after drinking, call 911. That's possible alcohol poisoning, and no drink fixes it.

## The Quick Timing Plan

If you want the short version before the explanation, here it is:

| When | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A few hours before | Eat a real meal with some salt, drink water as normal | Food slows alcohol absorption; you start the night topped up |
| Right before your first drink | A glass of water if you're thirsty | Arriving thirsty means your first drinks get gulped |
| While drinking | One glass of water or a low-sugar electrolyte drink between alcoholic drinks | Slows your pace and replaces some of what the kidneys are passing |
| Before bed | A glass of water or a modest electrolyte serving, plus a salty snack if you can | You're behind on fluid and about to go 7 to 8 hours without any |
| Next morning | Electrolyte drink or water plus a salty breakfast | Finish replacing what you lost overnight |
| Later that day | Keep drinking to thirst; watch your urine color | Pale yellow means you're caught up |

The rest of this page explains why the schedule looks like this, and when you can skip parts of it.

## What Your Kidneys Do When Alcohol Is On Board

To understand timing, it helps to know what alcohol actually does to your fluid balance, because it doesn't do the same thing all night.

### The rising phase: the kidneys let water go

Your kidneys are constantly deciding how much water to keep. The main signal they listen to is a hormone called **vasopressin** (also called antidiuretic hormone, or ADH), released from the base of the brain. When vasopressin is high, the kidneys hold onto water and your urine gets darker and more concentrated. When it's low, they let more water through and you pass more, paler urine.

Alcohol suppresses vasopressin. That's the main reason you "break the seal" at the bar: with less of the hold-onto-water signal, your kidneys let more fluid pass than they otherwise would. This effect has been studied since at least the 1940s, and later work from Ronald Maughan's group at Loughborough University and others has filled in the details.

An important detail that most hangover articles miss: this water-losing effect is strongest **while your blood alcohol is rising**, and it is fairly short-lived for each drink. Studies in the field have generally found that the extra urine shows up in the first few hours after drinking and then tapers off. Several also found that the effect is bigger with stronger drinks (spirits and wine) than with weaker ones, because you take in less water alongside the alcohol. With lower-strength beer, the water in the drink itself covers much of the extra urine.

### The falling phase: the kidneys swing back

Once you stop drinking and your blood alcohol starts to fall, vasopressin rebounds. The kidneys shift back into conserving mode and urine output drops. By the early morning, many people who were peeing constantly at the bar are making small amounts of dark urine. That dark urine isn't a sign that your kidneys are failing. It's a sign they're doing their job, holding on to water because you're now behind.

This swing matters for timing. Fluid you drink **while alcohol is still pouring in** is partly passed straight through. Fluid you drink **after you've stopped**, especially with some sodium, is more likely to stay put, because your kidneys are now trying to keep it.

### What else is being lost

Water isn't the only thing that leaves:

- **Sodium and chloride** go out with the extra urine, and with sweat if you were dancing or somewhere hot. These are the electrolytes that matter most for holding water in your body.
- **Potassium** losses are usually smaller but go up if you vomit.
- **Magnesium and calcium** are passed in larger amounts while alcohol is in your system. For an occasional drinker eating a normal diet, one night of this is easily made up by food over the next day or two. For people who drink heavily on a regular basis, low magnesium is a well-known problem that a doctor should look at, not something to fix with a sports drink.

### Where the alcohol itself goes

Your kidneys get rid of very little of the alcohol. Only a small percentage leaves unchanged through urine, breath, and sweat. The vast majority is broken down by the liver, first into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound, and then into acetate. A typical adult clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot from person to person. Nothing you drink speeds this up. Water and electrolytes don't flush alcohol out faster, because the liver, not the kidneys, sets the pace.

That's the heart of why rehydration has limits. It addresses the fluid your kidneys let go. It doesn't touch the acetaldehyde, the inflammation, or the wrecked sleep, which is where most of the hangover comes from.

## Before Drinking: Arrive Topped Up, Don't Pre-Load

There's a popular idea that you should load up on electrolytes before a night out, sometimes starting the day before. The logic sounds good: build a reserve, then spend it. Unfortunately, the body doesn't keep a reserve this way.

Your kidneys keep the sodium level in your blood in a tight range. If you drink a large dose of electrolytes at 3 p.m. when you're already well hydrated, your kidneys will mostly pass the extra salt and water out over the next few hours. By the time you have your third drink at 10 p.m., most of it is gone. You can't bank hydration for later the way you can charge a phone.

What does help before drinking:

- **Eat a real meal.** This is the single most useful thing you can do beforehand. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which lowers the peak blood alcohol your liver has to deal with. A meal with some salt in it also covers your sodium needs for the early part of the night. Our guide to [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) goes through which foods have the best evidence.
- **Don't arrive thirsty.** If you're thirsty when you get to the bar, your first couple of drinks get gulped to quench thirst rather than sipped. A glass of water before you head out avoids that.
- **Don't overdo plain water either.** Downing a liter of water right before you start drinking mostly gets you to the bathroom sooner. Drink to thirst.

### When a pre-drinking electrolyte drink does make sense

There are a few cases where having an electrolyte drink in the hours before drinking is reasonable:

- **You've been sweating heavily that day.** A hot outdoor event, a long hike, a workout, or a day at the beach means you're starting the night behind on both water and salt. Catching up beforehand is sensible.
- **You've been ill recently.** If you're recovering from a stomach bug, the honest advice is to skip drinking, but if you're going anyway, start properly rehydrated.
- **You know you won't eat much.** If the night involves drinks and very little food, a salty snack or an electrolyte drink at least gives you some sodium. Eating something is still better.

If you're looking at the bigger question of what to take or do before a night out, our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, and the guide to [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking) covers supplements specifically.

## During Drinking: The Glass Between Rounds

The classic advice to alternate each alcoholic drink with a glass of water is good advice. But it's worth being clear about why it works, because the main reason isn't hydration.

**It slows you down.** Hangover severity tracks how much alcohol you drink more closely than anything else. A glass of water between every drink roughly halves your drinking pace without much effort, which means lower peak blood alcohol and less total alcohol by the end of the night. That's a bigger benefit than the fluid itself.

**It does replace some fluid.** While your blood alcohol is rising and the kidneys are letting water go, a glass of water keeps some fluid coming in. Part of it will pass straight through, as explained above, but you'll still end the night less behind than if you'd drunk nothing but alcohol.

### Water or electrolytes during the night?

For most nights, plain water is fine. An electrolyte drink between rounds is a reasonable upgrade if:

- **You're sweating.** Dancing, a hot venue, an outdoor summer event. Sweat takes sodium with it, and alcohol adds to the water loss.
- **It's a long session.** An all-day wedding or festival, where you're drinking over many hours and maybe eating less than usual.
- **You prefer the taste.** If a lightly flavored drink means you'll actually have one between rounds, that's a fair reason.

Pick a **low-sugar** option if you go this route. A full-sugar sports drink between every alcoholic drink adds up to a lot of sugar over a night, and for some people a sugary stomach makes nausea worse later.

### Using electrolyte drinks as a mixer

Some people mix spirits with a sports drink or an electrolyte powder, hoping to hydrate and drink at the same time. It isn't harmful for a healthy person, but it doesn't do much either. The alcohol content is the same, and you're still taking in alcohol at the same rate. A sweet mixer can also make it easier to drink faster without noticing.

There's also an interesting wrinkle about sugar. Research led by Cecile Marczinski and colleagues found that people who drank alcohol mixed with diet soda reached higher breath alcohol levels than when the same alcohol was mixed with regular sugary soda, likely because sugar slows how fast the stomach empties. That isn't a reason to drink sugary cocktails. It's a reminder that food in your stomach is what really slows alcohol down, and that a separate glass of water is a better habit than relying on the mixer.

### What electrolytes can't do during the night

It's worth being blunt here because the marketing often isn't. Electrolyte drinks:

- **Don't lower your blood alcohol.** You'll be exactly as drunk with or without them.
- **Don't speed up alcohol clearance.** The liver sets the pace, at roughly one standard drink per hour.
- **Don't make it safe to drive** or to keep drinking past your limit.

## Before Bed: The Most Underrated Window

If you only do one thing on this list, make it a drink before bed. Here's why the timing works so well.

By the time you get home, three things are usually true. You've lost more fluid than you took in. You've stopped drinking, so your blood alcohol is starting to fall and your kidneys are shifting back to conserving water. And you're about to spend seven or eight hours drinking nothing at all. That makes bedtime the point where fluid you take in is most likely to stay in your body, and where the gap is about to get bigger if you do nothing.

What to have:

- **A glass of water, or a modest serving of an electrolyte drink.** One normal glass, maybe two. You don't need a liter.
- **A salty snack if you can face it.** Crackers, toast, a handful of pretzels. The salt helps your body hold onto the water, which is the whole idea behind oral rehydration. Food also helps if your blood sugar is low.
- **Sip it.** If you feel queasy, gulping a big drink is a good way to see it again. Small sips over ten minutes go down better.

Leave a glass of water or a bottle of electrolyte drink on your nightstand too. Waking at 4 a.m. with a dry mouth is common after drinking, and having something within reach makes it easy to sip without getting up.

Don't expect miracles, though. A bedtime glass of water makes the morning a bit gentler on the thirst and dry-mouth front. It does nothing about the poor sleep alcohol causes in the second half of the night (our [guide to alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains why), and it doesn't touch acetaldehyde or inflammation.

## The Morning After: Finish the Job

In the morning, you're usually still somewhat behind. Signs include thirst, a dry mouth, dark yellow urine, a headache that's worse when you stand, and feeling a little dizzy when you get up quickly. This is when a proper rehydration drink is most clearly worth it, especially in these cases:

- **You threw up.** Vomiting loses water, sodium, and potassium quickly, and it's exactly the situation oral rehydration drinks were designed for. Start with small sips every few minutes rather than a big glass, and build up as your stomach settles.
- **It was a long, heavy night.** More alcohol over more hours means a bigger deficit.
- **You can't face food.** Normally a salty breakfast delivers plenty of electrolytes. If eating isn't happening yet, a low-sugar electrolyte drink gets salt in without asking your stomach to digest a meal.

If none of those apply, water and a normal breakfast (eggs, toast, a banana) cover most people just as well for less money. Our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade guide](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) has the label numbers if you want to choose between the two most common options, and the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) page covers lower-sugar and medical-grade rehydration salts.

### How much to drink in the morning

There isn't a magic number. The practical guide is to drink steadily through the morning and watch your urine. Once it's back to pale yellow and you're no longer thirsty, you've caught up. Spreading drinks out works better than chugging a large volume at once, because the kidneys can only hold onto so much at a time and a big gulp on an unsettled stomach can come back up.

### Why the morning is better than "before" for electrolytes

This comes back to the kidneys. In the morning, your body is in conserving mode and you have a real deficit to fill. A rehydration drink with the right balance of sodium and a little sugar gets absorbed in the gut and held onto. Research on the "beverage hydration index," published by Maughan and colleagues in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* in 2016, found that an oral rehydration solution was retained in the body better than plain water over several hours, largely because of its sodium content. That retention advantage is most useful when you actually need the fluid, which is after drinking, not before.

## Electrolytes and Rehydration Only Cover Part of a Hangover

It's tempting to believe the story that alcohol dehydrates you, dehydration causes the hangover, and rehydration fixes it. The first part is true. The rest is only partly true.

Researchers who study hangovers, including the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, have generally found that measures of dehydration and blood electrolyte levels don't line up well with how bad people feel. You can be fully rehydrated and still feel awful. The bigger drivers of a hangover are:

- **How much you drank.** Total alcohol is the strongest predictor.
- **Acetaldehyde**, the toxic compound your liver makes as the first step in breaking alcohol down.
- **Inflammation.** Alcohol triggers the same immune messengers your body releases when you're sick, which is why a bad hangover can feel like the flu.
- **Poor sleep**, especially in the second half of the night.
- **Stomach irritation** and, for some people, **low blood sugar**.
- **Congeners**, byproducts found in larger amounts in darker drinks like bourbon and red wine.

So the timing plan above helps with one slice of the problem: the thirst, the dry mouth, the lightheadedness, and part of the headache. It won't fix the nausea, the fatigue, or the brain fog. Anyone who tells you that the right electrolyte schedule prevents hangovers is overselling it.

## Who Should Be Careful With Electrolyte Drinks

Electrolyte drinks are safe for most healthy adults in normal amounts, but they're designed to deliver sodium and potassium, and that isn't right for everyone.

- **Kidney disease.** Damaged kidneys may not clear extra potassium or sodium well. Check with your doctor before using rehydration drinks regularly.
- **Heart failure or high blood pressure.** If you've been told to limit salt, a few servings of a high-sodium drink can add up. Ask your doctor what's sensible for you.
- **Medicines that affect potassium.** Some blood pressure medicines (such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics) can raise potassium levels. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before adding potassium-rich drinks.
- **Diabetes.** Full-sugar sports drinks can affect blood sugar. Low-sugar options exist, and alcohol itself can cause low blood sugar, so follow the plan your care team has given you.

### The opposite problem: too much plain water

There's one situation where "just drink more water" is bad advice. Drinking very large amounts of plain water quickly, with no food and no salt, can dilute the sodium in your blood. This is called hyponatremia, and in serious cases it causes confusion, vomiting, and seizures. It's rare and takes real effort, but it's more likely when someone has lost a lot of fluid (for example from vomiting or heavy sweating) and then drinks liters of plain water with nothing else. The fix is simple: drink to thirst, spread it out, and pair water with some salt from food or a rehydration drink. Heavy beer drinking with very little food can cause a related problem, which is another reason to eat when you drink.

### When it's not a hangover anymore

Get medical help rather than relying on drinks at home if:

- You can't keep any fluids down for more than a day.
- You feel faint when you stand, or you're confused.
- You're passing very little urine many hours after drinking.
- You're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds.
- Symptoms last much longer than a normal hangover. Our guide to the [two-day hangover](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover) explains what's normal and what isn't.

## Putting It Together: A Sample Night

Here's how the timing plan might look for a typical evening out:

- **6:30 p.m.** Dinner with some salt in it. A glass of water.
- **8:00 p.m. to midnight.** One glass of water (or a low-sugar electrolyte drink if it's hot or you're dancing) between each alcoholic drink.
- **12:30 a.m.** Home. A glass of water or a small serving of an electrolyte drink, sipped, with a few crackers. Another glass on the nightstand.
- **8:00 a.m.** An electrolyte drink or water, plus breakfast. Keep sipping through the morning until you're no longer thirsty and your urine is pale.

Notice what does the heavy lifting: dinner beforehand and the glass between rounds keep your total alcohol and your peak blood alcohol down. The bedtime and morning drinks deal with the fluid deficit. Electrolyte drinks play a supporting role, not the lead.

If you like having everything ready before a big night, our [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas) page covers what's worth stocking.

## Where DHM Fits, Honestly

Everything above deals with fluid. If you want to go after the part of the hangover that rehydration can't reach, the place to look is how your body processes alcohol itself.

Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a plant extract from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, including the acetaldehyde step. The honest state of the evidence: encouraging animal and lab research, and limited human data. It's promising, not proven. It isn't a license to drink more, and it won't rescue a night of genuine excess. But unlike an electrolyte drink, it's at least aimed at the cause rather than the fluid loss.

On timing, DHM is usually taken before or during drinking, which makes it a natural partner to the bedtime-and-morning electrolyte routine rather than a replacement for it. If you want to try it, [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines 1,000 mg of DHM with L-cysteine and electrolytes, and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a budget pure-DHM option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- **After beats before.** Bedtime and the next morning are the most useful times for an electrolyte drink, because that's when you're actually behind and your kidneys are trying to hold on to water.
- **Before drinking, eat a real meal and don't arrive thirsty.** Pre-loading electrolytes hours ahead mostly gets passed in your urine.
- **During drinking, the glass between rounds works mainly by slowing you down.** Water is fine; a low-sugar electrolyte drink is a reasonable upgrade if you're sweating or it's a long session.
- **Alcohol makes the kidneys let water go while your blood alcohol is rising**, and they swing back to conserving once you stop. That's why fluid after drinking tends to stay put.
- **Rehydration helps with thirst, dry mouth, and part of the headache, not the whole hangover.** Total alcohol, acetaldehyde, inflammation, and poor sleep do most of the damage.
- **Check with your doctor first** if you have kidney disease, heart failure, high blood pressure, or take medicines that affect potassium.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it better to drink electrolytes before or after drinking alcohol?**

Both have a job, but they are different jobs. Before drinking, the goal is to start well hydrated and well fed, which a normal salty meal and a glass or two of water handle for most people. After drinking, especially before bed and the next morning, is when an electrolyte drink earns its place, because that is when you are actually behind on fluid. If you only do one, the bedtime and morning window gives you the most for your money.

**Should I drink electrolytes the night before drinking?**

There is no need to load up the night before. Your kidneys keep your sodium and fluid levels in a tight range, so extra electrolytes taken many hours ahead mostly end up in your urine. What helps is arriving at the night reasonably hydrated and having eaten a real meal in the few hours beforehand. That does more than any pre-loading routine.

**Does drinking electrolytes while drinking alcohol help?**

Mostly through the volume, not the salt. Alternating each drink with a glass of water or an electrolyte drink slows your pace and keeps some fluid coming in while alcohol is pushing it out. A low-sugar electrolyte drink is a reasonable choice for that glass, but plain water does most of the same job. Electrolytes do not lower your blood alcohol or stop you getting drunk.

**Should I drink electrolytes before bed after drinking?**

Yes, this is one of the most useful times. By bedtime you have usually lost more fluid than you took in, and you are about to spend seven or eight hours drinking nothing. A glass of water or a modest serving of an electrolyte drink with a salty snack lets you start the night less behind. Sip it rather than chugging, especially if you feel queasy, and don't force down huge amounts.

**How long after drinking should I take electrolytes?**

You can start as soon as you stop drinking. There is no waiting period, since electrolyte drinks do not interact with alcohol the way some medicines do. The practical schedule is a glass before bed, then a serving in the morning, with more through the day if you were sick, sweated a lot, or are still very thirsty with dark urine.

**Can you mix electrolyte drinks with alcohol?**

You can, and it isn't dangerous for a healthy person, but it doesn't cancel out the alcohol. A sports drink used as a mixer still delivers the same amount of alcohol, and sugary mixers can make it easier to drink faster without noticing. A separate glass of water or electrolytes between drinks is a better habit than mixing them in.

**Do electrolytes prevent a hangover?**

No. They help with the part of a hangover that comes from losing fluid, such as thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and some of the headache. Research on hangovers has generally found that dehydration and electrolyte levels do not explain most of how bad people feel. The bigger drivers are how much alcohol you drank, its breakdown products like acetaldehyde, inflammation, and poor sleep.

**Who should be careful with electrolyte drinks after drinking?**

People with kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure who have been told to limit sodium or potassium should check with their doctor before using electrolyte drinks regularly, because these products are designed to deliver those minerals. The same goes for anyone on medicines that affect potassium, such as some blood pressure drugs. If you can't keep fluids down for more than a day, get medical help rather than relying on drinks at home.
